title: Influence of Ti-, Nb- and Ti + Nb-based microalloying concepts on HAZ behaviour and local mechanical performance of welded S690QL steel
abstract: Abstract High-strength, quenched and tempered steels, such as S690QL, require specific microalloying concepts to achieve the necessary balance of strength, toughness and weldability. As the mechanical integrity of welded structures is significantly impacted by the behaviour of the heat-affected zone (HAZ) during welding, a thorough understanding of microstructural evolution is crucial. This study systematically investigates the effect of Ti or Nb microalloying as well as a combination of both on three-layer gas metal arc welded joints. Metallographic characterisation, hardness mapping and thermophysical simulations are employed to determine the interaction between precipitate stability, austenite grain growth and softened HAZ formation. Cross-weld tensile tests combined with digital image correlation (DIC) enable the in situ monitoring of local strain accumulation in critical microstructural zones. A mirror-assisted optical setup enables the simultaneous evaluation of strain on multiple specimen surfaces, providing comprehensive insight into constraint effects and the mechanisms controlling strain localisation and fracture initiation. Complementary impact toughness measurements further highlight the influence of microalloying and dilution on fracture behaviour in both the HAZ and the weld metal. The combined findings demonstrate that the microalloying strategy governs the extent of HAZ softening, the distribution of local strain and the failure mechanisms within the weldment. Specifically, the interaction between Ti- and Nb-containing precipitates plays a significant role in HAZ microstructure formation and local mechanical response enhancement. In summary, the results indicate that a combination of Ti and Nb microalloying is the most effective approach to enhancing the local mechanical performance and toughness, improving the integrity of the HAZ in S690QL steel welds.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: High-strength low-alloy (HSLA) steels with nominal yield strengths ≥ 690 MPa have been widely used across various industries [ 1 ]. Their combination of high strength and adequate ductility is achieved in part through the addition of microalloying elements such as Ti, Nb and V. The compositional limits for these steels are specified in EN 10025-6 [ 2 ], which defines the maximum allowable content for each element. Due to the high possible ratio of yield strength to ultimate tensile strength and the requirement to maintain specific microstructures such as bainite or martensite in the HAZ, these steels must be welded carefully within narrow parameter windows [ 2 ,  3 – 4 ]. However, this flexibility complicates the assessment of weldability, since individual steel manufacturers may independently select the specific contents of Ti, Nb and/or V within the permitted limits. As a result, differing microalloying strategies arise, which in turn lead to variations in welding behaviour. The manufacturing objective is to adjust the mechanical and technological properties of a given HSLA steel through appropriate microalloying. However, numerous studies have demonstrated that the weldability of these steels is highly dependent on the specific microalloying strategy. Traditional weldability assessment concepts, such as the carbon equivalent (CE), are of limited use, as they generally do not consider microalloying elements and primarily describe hardenability or cold-cracking susceptibility.

Prior investigations have shown that Nb-microalloyed steels exhibit enhanced tempering resistance and therefore do not experience pronounced softening in the intercritical and subcritical HAZ (ICHAZ and SCHAZ) [ 3 ,  4 ]. This behaviour can be explained by the synergistic interaction between Mo and Nb, which retards martensite decomposition in tempering regions and thus mitigates HAZ softening during welding. In contrast, Ti-microalloyed steels show limited tempering resistance and develop significant softening in the IC- and SCHAZ [ 5 ,  6 ]. This effect also depends on the Ti content; earlier studies indicated that higher Ti additions can be more beneficial for the mechanical performance of the welded joint than low Ti levels [ 5 ]. Moreover, the stoichiometric Ti/N ratio plays a crucial role in the pinning effect and, consequently, in controlling austenite grain (AG) growth and the formation of the coarse-grained HAZ (CGHAZ) [ 5 ,  7 ,  8 ]. Previous work on Ti + V microalloyed S690QL steels also revealed beneficial effects on weld integrity, as such combinations shift phase transformation to lower temperatures, improving tempering resistance [ 6 ,  9 ]. Additionally, local mechanical analyses during cross-weld tensile testing have shown pronounced constraint effects. However, the transfer of commonly used parameters, such as the relative thickness of the softened zone ( X sz  < 0.25) as a threshold for preventing failure, appears to be strongly influenced by weld geometry and the relative position of the softened region [ 5 ].

The present study investigates the influence of Ti-, Nb- and Ti + Nb-based microalloying concepts on the HAZ behaviour and local mechanical performance of welded S690QL steel. For this reason, thermodynamic simulations and thermophysical experiments were performed to evaluate precipitate stability, grain boundary pinning and austenite grain growth behaviour. Furthermore, three-layer welds were produced and characterised with respect to their microstructure and hardness distribution. The global mechanical properties of the welded joints were assessed by cross-weld tensile testing. In addition, DIC was employed to analyse the local deformation behaviour of the individual weld regions, with particular focus on the HAZ and weld metal (WM). Supplementary Charpy impact tests were conducted on specimens extracted from the HAZ and WM, and the resulting toughness values were correlated with the local strain distributions obtained by DIC.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
paragraphs: The overall experimental procedure applied in this study is summarised in Fig.  1 . The workflow comprises the production and characterisation of four differently microalloyed S690QL steel grades, followed by thermodynamic simulations, three-layer MAG welding and complementary thermophysical simulations. Subsequently, the welded joints were subjected to microstructural characterisation, hardness measurements and mechanical testing. Finally, the obtained results were correlated to evaluate the influence of different Ti- and Nb-based microalloying concepts on HAZ softening, local strain localisation and toughness behaviour. Fig. 1 Experimental workflow for evaluating the influence of Ti- and Nb-based microalloying concepts on welded S690QL steel

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: For a systematic assessment of the influence of different microalloying strategies on the weldability, four laboratory heats were produced and subsequently subjected to an identical heat treatment (kindly delivered by voestalpine Grobblech GmbH, Linz, Austria). The investigated microalloying strategies were selected based on current knowledge regarding the influence of Ti and Nb on the weldability and HAZ behaviour of high-strength quenched and tempered steels. Previous studies have demonstrated that Nb can improve tempering resistance and reduce HAZ softening, whereas Ti-containing precipitates provide effective pinning of austenite grain boundaries due to their high thermal stability [ 6 ,  10 ]. Consequently, four laboratory heats were designed to systematically isolate the individual effects of Ti and Nb as well as their combined interaction. The selected alloying contents were chosen within the compositional limits specified by EN 10025-6 [ 2 ] and in cooperation with the steel manufacturer to represent technically relevant microalloying strategies for S690QL steels.

The first heat corresponded to a conventional S690QL grade in the quenched and tempered (Q + T) condition and served as a reference material (‘Ref.’). Within the limits [ 2 ], the Ti and Nb content was systematically varied for three further heats. Hence, four different S690QL grades could be investigated as base materials (BMs). The chemical composition, in accordance with [ 2 ], is provided in Table  1 . The reference condition (‘Ref.’) contained neither Ti nor Nb. Alloy Grade ‘A’ represented a Nb-microalloyed grade, while grade ‘B’ corresponded to the Ti-microalloyed condition. Grade ‘C’ was designed as an approach of combined Ti + Nb microalloying. The element quantification analysis was carried out using optical emission spectroscopy (OES, Spectro LabM, SPECTRO Analytical Instruments GmbH, Germany). The nitrogen and oxygen contents of the BMs were determined by carrier gas hot extraction (CGHE, G8 Galileo analyser, Bruker AXS, Germany). For comparison, the nominal composition of the S690QL (in accordance with [ 2 ]) is also provided in Table  1 , together with the chemical composition of the solid wire weld metal (WM) as reported by the manufacturer.

sections.heading: Modified spray arc MAG welding
paragraphs: Three-layer welds were produced under free shrinkage conditions by means of automated metal active gas (MAG) welding (using an Alpha Q 552 power source, EWM GmbH, Germany). The experimental setup involved plates with dimensions of 300 mm × 150 mm, prepared with a V-groove geometry. The joint configuration featured a total opening angle of 30°; see Fig.  2 . Fig. 2 Seam layer setup of a three-layer weld

To provide uniform thermal conditions during welding, both preheating and interpass temperatures were maintained at 100 °C. Shielding was achieved with an M21 gas mixture (DIN EN ISO 14175 [ 11 ]). The welding parameters were determined based on preliminary welding trials conducted prior to the experimental programme. Welding was carried out at a welding speed ‘ v s ’ of 400 mm/min in direct current (DC) polarity, with current values between 262 and 280 A and an arc voltage from 24 to 26 V (resulting in a modified spray arc). Under these conditions, the average welding heat input ‘ Q ’ was 1 kJ/mm. The cooling time Δ t 8/5  was approximately 7.8 s (measured via laser pyrometer, Lumasense RS485, Imc Messsysteme GmbH, Germany).

sections.heading: Metallographic investigations and complementary analyses
paragraphs: Metallographic specimens were sectioned transverse to the welding direction from the weld centreline, embedded, ground, polished to 1 µm, and etched with 2 wt.% Nital. The HAZ microstructure was analysed by SEM (Phenom XL, 15 kV), while fracture surfaces of cross-weld tensile specimens were examined with a Tescan Vega 3 XLH SEM (20 kV) equipped with an EDS detector for precipitate characterization.

Hardness mapping was carried out on polished cross sections using the UCI method (ISO 50159-1 [ 12 ]) with an applied load of 4.903 N (HV0.5). Furthermore, these hardness mappings were analysed using MATLAB R2022a to enable quantitative evaluation of the hardness. Additional HV1 hardness profiles (ISO 6507-1 [ 13 ]) were recorded along the weld layers with indentation spacing of 0.5 mm in the WM and BM and 0.25 mm in the HAZ. Additionally, a statistical analysis within the HAZ as a function of the individual microalloying concepts was carried out (using the software Design-Expert, V22.0.1, Stat-Ease, Inc., USA).

The thermodynamic simulations were performed using ThermoCalc® 2025a with the ‘TCFE11’ and ‘MOBFE6’ databases. Equilibrium phase diagrams and precipitate volume fractions were calculated for the investigated BMs between 500 and 2000 °C.

To evaluate the austenite grain growth behaviour of the individual microalloying concepts, dilatometry experiments were conducted using a TA Instruments DIL 805 A/D dilatometer under partial vacuum during heating and nitrogen atmosphere for defined cooling. Peak temperatures ‘ T p ’ between 1000 and 1200 °C were applied using a constant heating time of 5 s, followed by holding time of 3 s at ‘ T p ’ and a Δ t 8/5  time of 10 s. These peak temperatures were selected to ensure complete austenitisation above A c3  and to investigate austenite grain growth under controlled conditions. Subsequently, the hardness (HV1) according to [ 13 ] and the mean grain diameter were determined by the linear intercept method [ 14 ].

sections.heading: Cross-weld tensile samples and local DIC strain measurement
paragraphs: Flat transverse tensile specimens were extracted from the centre of the welded 300 × 300 mm plates, ensuring that mainly the filling layer was tested. The geometry followed ISO 4136 [ 15 ], with a gage length of 70 mm and a thickness of 5 mm (Fig.  3 b). Testing was conducted on a 250 kN servo-hydraulic machine (Schenck GmbH, Germany) under displacement control at a strain rate of 2.5 × 10 –5  s −1 . To enable in situ strain monitoring during the tensile test, a digital image correlation (DIC) system (ARAMIS, Zeiss, Germany—with a stereo camera setup, each with a resolution of 12 MP) was employed at an acquisition rate of 1 Hz. After applying a preload of 1 kN, the camera system was activated, and the load–displacement data was recorded via the ‘InstronConsole’ and ‘Instron Wavemaker’, both by Instron GmbH, Germany. For reliable correlation, a stochastic black-on-white speckle pattern was manually applied. To capture the strain response on three specimen surfaces (root, top layer and thickness), the DIC setup was extended with a custom-built mirror fixture consisting of two aluminium-coated surface mirrors (85 × 60 mm); see Fig.  3 a. The experiments were conducted three times under identical conditions for each welded grade. Fig. 3 Mechanical testing:  a  test setup for quasi-static cross-weld tensile tests with strain monitoring via DIC and surface mirrors,  b  specimen geometry of cross-weld tensile specimen and  c  schematic illustration of V-notched impact specimens extraction locations from the welded plate

This setup allowed simultaneous evaluation of strain development across multiple regions of the weld. Data were processed using GOM Correlate software, with strain paths set along the y-direction transverse to the weld seam as well as across defined sectional planes. Particular attention was given to strain distribution directly before fracture.

All tensile tests were conducted under laboratory conditions at an ambient temperature of approximately 25 ± 2 °C. The relative humidity was not actively controlled during testing but remained within the typical indoor laboratory range. Since all specimens were tested under identical environmental conditions, no significant influence on the comparative evaluation of the investigated microalloying concepts is expected.

sections.heading: Fracture toughness
paragraphs:
Charpy V-notch impact tests were also conducted to evaluate the toughness of the WM, HAZ and BM (see results in Table  2 ). For each investigated microalloying strategy, three specimens were machined from the respective regions (Fig.  3 c), with the HAZ notches positioned after prior etching to ensure correct placement. All samples were taken from mid-plate thickness and tested at −40 °C in accordance with EN ISO 148-1:2017 [ 16 ], using a HIT750P pendulum impact tester (Zwick Roell GmbH, Germany).

sections.heading: Phase equilibrium and metallographic characterisation of microalloyed steel grades
paragraphs: Figure  4  presents a comparison of the four investigated microalloying concepts with respect to their differences in microstructure, hardness, grain size, and equilibrium phase fractions in the temperature range between 500 and 2000 °C. All four microalloying concepts contain corundum (Al 3 O 2 ), which forms in the liquid phase during steel production at temperatures between approximately 1930 and 1970 °C. Metallographic analysis revealed that the reference alloy, which does not contain classical microalloying elements such as Ti, Nb or V, exhibits the largest mean grain diameter of 17 µm compared to the microalloyed concepts containing Ti and/or Nb. In the austenitic phase, AlN precipitates at around 1190 °C and increases in volume fraction to approximately 4.5 × 10 –4  mol as the temperature decreases to 500 °C. Grade A (Nb), on the other hand, exhibits a mean grain diameter of 13 µm, indicating effective AG boundary pinning by Nb-precipitates. In grade A (Nb), both AlN and Nb(C,N) precipitates form under equilibrium conditions at approximately 1180 °C, reaching a volume fraction of 6.5 × 10  − 4  mol at 500 °C. The Ti-microalloyed concept (grade B) shows an even stronger influence on AG growth, resulting in a finer mean grain size of 12 µm. In grade B (Ti), TiN precipitates form at around 1490 °C, indicating the high thermal stability of these precipitates. Grade C represents a combination of the characteristics of A and B. In terms of grain size refinement and BM hardness, the Ti + Nb microalloyed steel exhibits behaviour comparable to that of the Ti-microalloyed steel. Under equilibrium conditions, TiN precipitates form at 1481 °C, while NbC precipitates appear at around 1150 °C. At 500 °C, the volume fraction of NbC precipitates is approximately 27 times higher than that of TiN precipitates. However, it can be assumed that in this multicomponent system, complex Ti,Nb(C,N) precipitates may form under non-equilibrium conditions. Fig. 4 SEM micrographs and equilibrium phase diagrams of BMs:  a ,  b  reference grade,  c ,  d  grade A (Nb),  e ,  f  grade B (Ti) and  g ,  h  grade C (Ti + Nb)

sections.heading: Thermophysical simulation of austenite grain growth
paragraphs: To obtain the understanding of the AG pinning as a function of different microalloying concepts, austenitisation experiments were conducted using a quenching dilatometer. Information on austenite grain growth not only provides insight into the microstructural evolution within the HAZ exposed to austenitisation temperatures but also offers an understanding of the microstructural behaviour in terms of the thermal stability of precipitates and the continuity of the phase transformation itself. Figure  5  presents the results of the investigations on AG growth as a function of three different peak temperatures. The AG growth behaviour is strongly influenced by the peak temperature, heating rate, holding time, cooling rate and the presence of precipitates, which themselves exhibit varying thermal stabilities. As expected, the AG size increases with rising peak temperature for all microalloying concepts. This behaviour can be attributed to the higher grain boundary mobility at elevated temperatures and the reduced pinning force against grain growth, caused by the coarsening and partial dissolution of precipitates during the thermal cycle. It was observed that microalloy precipitates dissolve, reprecipitate and undergo coarsening due to the Ostwald ripening effect during the thermal process [ 17 ]. The behaviour of these precipitates, depending on their thermal stability and the attained peak temperature, has a significant influence on the grain growth rate and the resulting final grain size. Fig. 5 AG growth as a function of peak temperature for the four investigated microalloying concepts:  a  mean grain diameter and  b  hardness HV1

The reference grade exhibited only a marginal effect in restricting AG growth at elevated temperatures, a phenomenon that can be attributed to the absence of Ti and/or Nb precipitates [ 18 ]. At a peak temperature of 1200 °C, the addition of Nb is observed to reduce the average AG diameter by around 47% compared to the reference grade. The addition of Ti resulted in a reduction of the AG size by approximately 70% at 1200 °C compared to the reference condition (‘ref.’) without Ti or Nb microalloying. The combined addition of Ti and Nb (grade C) shows a similar effect to grade B (Ti), leading to a reduction in AG size of about 68%. Furthermore, it can be observed that grades B and C show minor changes in AG size at elevated temperatures compared to the other two investigated grades, indicating the high thermal stability of their precipitates. In this context, the AG size increases by a factor of 2.3 for grade B and 2.7 for grade C when the temperature rose from 1000 to 1200 °C. Meanwhile, grade A showed an increase by a factor of 3.7, and the reference grade exhibited the largest change in AG size by a factor > 4.4.

The resulting hardness distribution should be interpreted with caution, as the measured hardness values exhibit considerable scatter. However, the mean values show that grade C exhibits the most pronounced hardening compared to the as-received condition within the temperature range between 1000 and 1200 °C (see Fig.  4 g). In the base condition (303 HV1), the hardness increases to an average value of 351 HV1 after treatment at  T p  = 1200 °C with a Δ t 8/5  cooling time of 10 s, corresponding to an increase of approximately 16%. Based on the comparable grain size distribution to that of grade C, it could be expected that grade B, which is microalloyed solely with Ti, would exhibit a similar hardness behaviour. The hardness analysis contradicts this assumption and instead reveals a lower hardness for grade B at 1200 °C (343 HV1) compared to grade C (Ti + Nb). Nevertheless, grade B (Ti) still exhibits a hardening of approximately 13% relative to the as-received condition (see Fig.  4 e). In contrast, grade A (Nb) showed a slight softening (between 1 and 3%) after high-temperature heat treatment compared to the as-received condition (348 HV1). The reference grade exhibited a hardening at 1200 °C (similar to grade C), with an increase of approximately 12% relative to the as-received condition.

The presented results can be transferred to the behaviour of the CGHAZ during welding. They suggest that there is a divergent response in terms of phase transformation, grain size and hardness distribution within the CGHAZ for the different microalloying concepts.

sections.heading: Hardness distribution across the welded joints
paragraphs: The HV0.5 hardness distributions of all weld joints measured using the UCI method are shown in Fig.  6 a–d. Each subfigure presents the hardness profiles on the left and the corresponding cross sections on the right. All four steel grades exhibit a clear hardness reduction in the intercritical (IC-) and subcritical (SC-) HAZ. Fig. 6 UCI hardness distribution and quantitative analysis of the hardness mapping, used to determine the hardness distribution within each individual weld layer (refer to the black, blue and red marked lines in  a ):  a ,  b  reference grade,  c ,  d  grade A (Nb),  e ,  f  grade B (Ti) and  g ,  h  grade C (Ti + Nb)

The UCI hardness mapping was primarily used to qualitatively assess the metallurgical changes within the HAZ. Here, ‘softening’ and ‘hardening’ refer to local hardness variations linked to the respective microstructures. The softening zone, characterised by reduced hardness, is highlighted in blue in Fig.  6 a–d. To enable quantitative assessment of the hardness distribution along individual weld layers, measurement lines were applied to the UCI hardness matrix using MATLAB (see the marked lines in the UCI hardness map in Fig.  6 a). The corresponding evaluations of these measurement lines are presented in Fig.  6 e–h, aligned with the respective UCI mappings. The minimum UCU hardness values in the respective weld layers and the maximum hardness in top layers are presented in Fig.  6 e–h.

Based on [ 5 ,  19 ,  20 ], softening mechanisms are distinguished by the peak temperature in the welding thermal cycle: Tempering softening is observed below A c1 -temperature, while transformation softening is exhibited above it. In quenched and tempered steels, the deterioration of hardness in the HAZ is predominantly attributable to the process of tempering. Precipitation-hardening elements may either enhance softening by causing the formation of larger precipitates or reduce it by forming smaller new precipitates [ 4 ,  21 ].

From the quantitative evaluation of the UCI hardness mappings, the following conclusions can be drawn: The reference grade, whose softening mechanisms in the IC- and SCHAZ can be attributed to pronounced tempering effects, exhibits a relatively large CGHAZ with an area of 6.1 mm 2  and a maximum UCI hardness of 382 HV0.5; see (Fig.  6 a, e). In comparison, the hardness in the IC- and SCHAZ of the top layer decreases by 35%, reaching 247 HV0.5 (UCI). This behaviour is consistent with the observations from the dilatometric AG growth simulations (Fig.  5 ). Due to the absence of microalloying elements such as Ti and Nb, the pinning effect that counteracts AG growth is weak, leading to an enlarged CGHAZ. The hardness reduction in the IC- and SCHAZ of both the root and top layer of the reference grade is therefore attributed to tempering effects induced by the subsequent weld layers.

The hardness in the as-received condition of grade A (Nb) is up to 45 HV1 higher than that of grade C (see Fig.  4 ). Consequently, the UCI hardness mapping of grade A (Nb) shows a red-coloured region in the BM, as the legend of the UCI map was calibrated to the reference grade. Nevertheless, the CGHAZ area is 5.3 mm 2  and has a maximum hardness of 402 HV0.5 (UCI) (Fig.  6 b, f). The size of the CGHAZ is consistent with the results of the AG growth simulations. Grade A (Nb) exhibits the next highest pinning effect on AG boundaries after the reference specimen, as shown in Fig.  5 a. However, the interpretation of the UCI hardness mapping must be approached with caution, as the quantitative hardness assessment appears to suggest a ‘hardening’ effect in the CGHAZ of the top layer and a corresponding ‘softening’ in the outer HAZ regions. Such conclusions cannot be drawn directly, since conventional Vickers HV1 measurements of the BM and thermophysically simulated specimens indicate that softening rather than hardening would be expected in the CGHAZ compared to the BM (see Sect.  3.1 ). This highlights a limitation that requires the UCI hardness mapping to be interpreted carefully and makes direct comparison more difficult, even when using a consistent colour scale.

Grade B (Ti) (Fig.  6 c, g) exhibits a very narrow CGHAZ with an area of 3.6 mm 2 . The thermally stable Ti precipitates, which dissolve only near their equilibrium temperature of approximately 1490 °C (see Fig.  4 f), provide an excellent pinning effect on the AG boundaries. This is consistent with the results shown in Fig.  5 a. However, the maximum UCI hardness measured in the CGHAZ is the lowest of all microalloying concepts investigated, at 366 HV0.5 (UCI). This finding correlates well with the hardness results of the AG growth simulations (Fig.  5 b). Across the entire plate thickness, the hardness in the IC- and SCHAZ is also the lowest of all microalloying concepts, ranging between 229 and 239 HV0.5 (UCI), indicating a very limited tempering resistance of this microalloying strategy.

Grade C (Ti + Nb) also exhibits a very narrow CGHAZ in the cap pass, with an area of 4.1 mm 2 , along with relatively good tempering resistance in the outer HAZ regions across the entire plate thickness (Fig.  6 d). Moreover, concept C, which essentially represents a combination of concepts A and B, shows pronounced hardening in the CGHAZ, with a maximum UCI hardness of 418 HV0.5 (see Fig.  6 h). These observations from the UCI hardness mapping are consistent with the AG growth simulation results presented in Fig.  5 a, b.

The HV1 hardness data were statistically analysed to assess the effect of different microalloying strategies on softening behaviour. Only the minimum HV1 hardness measured in the HAZ of the fill pass was considered for this purpose (see blue-marked line in Fig.  6 a). Furthermore, the statistical analysis of the minimum HAZ hardness in the fill passes shown in Fig.  7  applies exclusively to the welding parameters described in Sect.  2.2 . To achieve statistical significance, all available microalloying concepts were included in the evaluation. However, this study focuses solely on the data points indicated by the white arrows in Fig.  7 a, b. These data points represent the mass-percent levels of Ti and Nb (see also Table  1 ) in the respective microalloying concepts investigated. The statistical model yields a  p  value of 0.05 and is therefore statistically significant. Fig. 7 Statistical evaluation of the minimum hardness measured in the weld filler layer (softening zone) as a function of the microalloying concept (points marked with arrows indicate the microalloying concepts presented in this study):  a  contour plot and  b  3D view and results from statistical the model

A hardness map is shown in a 2D planar view (Fig.  7 a) and as a 3D representation with corresponding isolines of hardness (Fig.  7 b). Using these lines, the minimum HAZ hardness in the fill layer can be calculated for any Ti/Nb content configuration by means of the equation provided below Fig.  7 b. From Fig.  7 a, it can be observed that grade A exhibits the highest minimum HV1 hardness, whereas the lowest minimum hardness in the HAZ of the fill layer is found in the reference grade and in the microalloying strategy corresponding to high Ti and Nb content (upper right corner in Fig.  7 a). The intensive softening predicted for the theoretical microalloying concept can be attributed to the solubility of Ti and Nb in Fe [ 22 ]. At elevated concentrations of Ti and Nb, the formation of fine precipitates like carbonitrides is stopped and replaced by segregation or cluster formation of µm-scale inclusions instead, which provide only little contribution to precipitation strengthening and do not effectively limit the AG growth. This, in turn, would reduce the tempering resistance. As a result, the hardness would decline to values even lower than those of the reference grade, which contains no microalloying elements. For this reason, excessive additions of Ti and Nb (more precise: the individual stochiometric ratio to Fe, N and C) have an opposite effect on the weld integrity (see three-layer welds in Sect.  2.2 ).

sections.heading: Global mechanical performance in cross-weld tensile testing
paragraphs: The overall mechanical tensile behaviour in as-welded condition is illustrated in Fig.  8 a, presented as exemplary engineering stress–strain curves. The ultimate tensile strength (UTS,  R m  in MPa) and the maximum strain ( ε max  in %) were evaluated. Cross-weld tensile specimens do not permit a reliable determination of the global yield strength of the welded joint, owing to the well-established heterogeneous local deformation across the weldment, particularly within the HAZ. Nevertheless, a global virtual 0.2% proof stress ( R p0.2 , in MPa) was calculated and used as an assessment criterion for the mechanical performance of the welded joint. Fig. 8 a  Exemplary global stress strain curves for each steel grade investigated and DIC strain distribution in the y-direction shortly before fracture of  b  reference grade,  c  grade A (Nb),  d  grade B (Ti) and  e  grade C (Ti + Nb)

As illustrated in Fig.  8 a, all four BMs in welded condition exhibited comparable mechanical performance during tensile loading. After exceeding the UTS, the corresponding strain localisation occurred consistently within the HAZ and/or along the fusion line. In Fig.  8 b–e, the corresponding DIC images are presented, depicting the y-direction strain distribution shortly before fracture (individual end-near region of the stress–strain curves in Fig.  7 a). The resulting highly concentrated local deformation ultimately promoted fracture initiation at these sites.

Table  3  presents the global tensile properties obtained from cross-weld tensile specimens, reported as arithmetic mean values with standard deviations. The 0.2% proof stress ( R p0.2 ) varies between 725 ± 3 MPa for grade B (Ti) and 745 ± 1 MPa for grade C (Ti + Nb). The ultimate tensile strength ( R m ) shows a similarly narrow range, from 829 ± 3 MPa (grade B (Ti)) to 848 ± 8 MPa (grade C (Ti + Nb)). The maximum elongation ( ε max ) exhibits slightly greater scatter, with values from 6.5 ± 0.2% for the reference grade to 7.8 ± 1.3% for grade C (Ti + Nb). These results indicate that all investigated grades demonstrate comparable global tensile performance, with only moderate variations in strength and ductility.

Figure  9 a to –d displays the fracture surface topographies of four representative cross-weld tensile specimens examined for each steel grade. All investigated tensile samples failed primarily by ductile fracture, evidenced by the presence of microvoid coalescence and the resulting dimpled surface morphology. In the reference grade (Fig.  9 a), a pronounced shear orientation is visible, producing elongated shear dimples aligned with the local maximum shear stress. Grade A (Nb) (Fig.  9 b) displays a fine dimpled structure, consistent with Nb-related microstructural refinement. In both the reference and grade A (Nb), EDX analysis revealed AlO-containing inclusions within the dimples. This observation is consistent with the use of Al as a deoxidizing element, which binds dissolved oxygen and promotes the formation of alumina-based inclusions [ 23 ]. Grade B (Ti) (Fig.  9 c) shows larger and partially elongated dimples, suggesting localised strain accumulation. Inclusions are likewise visible within the larger dimples; however, their chemical composition could not be conclusively identified by EDX. Such inclusions may act as initiation sites for microcracks, functioning as micro-notches that generate locally elevated stress concentrations under mechanical loading. In addition, their relatively weak interfacial bonding to the surrounding ferritic matrix can promote particle–matrix debonding, thereby facilitating early microcrack formation and subsequent fracture propagation [ 24 ,  25 ]. Fig. 9 Fracture surface topographies of cross-weld tensile specimens with corresponding EDX maps of large inclusions identified:  a  reference grade,  b  grade A (Nb),  c  grade B (Ti) and  d  grade C (Ti + Nb)

In contrast, grade C (Ti + Nb) additionally reveals regions of quasi-cleavage fracture, typically observed in macroscopically undeformed, quenched-and-tempered steels with fracture planes perpendicular to the principal tensile stress. Nevertheless, isolated dimples remain detectable, indicating a mixed ductile–brittle fracture mode.

sections.heading: Local strain behaviour in cross-weld specimens by DIC
paragraphs: Figure  10 a–d presents an exemplary distribution of the local principal strain ( ε y  in %) in the y-direction for the respective steel grades along a sectional plane located at the centre of the top, V-seam (specimen thickness) and root layer of the cross-weld tensile specimen (corresponding to Fig.  3 a). Of particular interest in this context was the strain distribution shortly before fracture. Distinct constraint effects are evident from the strain distribution. The pronounced metallurgical gradient in the y-direction causes mechanically weaker regions—such as the softened fusion line and the severely softened sub-zones of the HAZ (e.g. ICHAZ and SCHAZ)—to be mechanically restrained by adjacent zones of higher strength, including the locally hardened HAZ regions, the WM and the unaffected BM. This interaction accounts for the characteristic decrease followed by a subsequent increase in the local strain across these regions. However, this pronounced constraint effect is observed predominantly on the top-layer side, where the weld is wider. This observation is consistent with previous findings [ 5 ], which demonstrated that weld geometry (and in particular the weld seam angle) significantly influences the mechanical performance. A wider weld, and thus a different orientation and distribution of the softened HAZ regions, promotes more effective mechanical support compared with a narrower weld. Consequently, the geometric configuration enhances the constraint conditions acting on the softened zones [ 5 ]. Fig. 10 Exemplary distribution of localised principal strain in y-direction along sectional plane length at the positions top pass, V-seam and pass:  a  reference grade,  b  grade A (Nb),  c  grade B (Ti) and grade C (Ti + Nb)

In contrast, the investigated microalloying concepts generally show pronounced strain accumulation in the root region shortly before fracture, which also corresponds to the location of crack initiation. However, the highest local strains in the y-direction are observed on the root side for grade A (Nb), reaching 97%, and for grade C (Ti + Nb), reaching 115% (see Fig.  10 b, d). This behaviour is also evident in the microalloying concepts that exhibit higher tempering resistance and show no pronounced softening in the outer HAZ regions, such as grade B (Ti) and the reference grade (see also Figs.  6  and  7 ). These observations are consistent with the global mechanical parameters summarised in Table  3 , including  ε max  and  R m . The reference grade and grade B (Ti) failed within the HAZ or fusion zone, which is consistent with the pronounced softening observed in the fusion zone (see Fig.  6 a, c). In contrast, grades A (Nb) and C (Ti + Nb) do not exhibit a clearly identifiable fracture location; however, it is assumed that failure occurred either along the fusion line or within the WM.

The observed strain localisation corresponded closely to the subsequent fracture locations, indicating that DIC provides a valuable tool for identifying mechanically critical regions and potential fracture initiation sites within welded joints.

sections.heading: Local strain vs. impact toughness of WM and HAZ
paragraphs: Figure  11  presents a comparison between the Charpy impact toughness and the maximum local strain in the y-direction obtained from the cross-weld tensile test shortly before fracture. Figure  11 a clearly illustrates the influence of microalloying strategy on the impact toughness within the HAZ. Grade C (Ti + Nb) exhibits an impact energy exceeding 148 J, whereas the reference grade shows a considerably lower toughness of 82 J in the HAZ. These high impact‐toughness values are consistent with the reduced hardness gradient observed in grade C (Ti + Nb) along the fill layer (see Fig.  6 d, h). In addition, grade C (Ti + Nb) exhibits a much finer and harder microstructure in the CGHAZ, as indicated by the simulated AG growth shown in Fig.  5 a, b. The combined microalloying with Ti and Nb thus merges the beneficial effects of both elements: Ti contributing to grain refinement and Nb enhancing tempering resistance. Considering the local strain in the HAZ shortly before fracture in the quasi-static cross-weld tensile test, a similar trend was observed. Grade C (Ti + Nb) exhibited the highest local strain in the HAZ, exceeding 80% relative to the initial gauge length. Grade B (Ti) reached strain levels above 70%, while grade A (Nb) shows local strains above 40%. Fig. 11 Comparison of CVN energy and local principal strain ε y  shortly before fracture for all investigated microalloying strategies:  a  HAZ and  b  WM

Examining the local mechanical properties within the WM revealed a clear trend. The reference grade exhibited the lowest impact toughness at 67 J, followed by grade A (Nb) at 77 J and grade C (Ti + Nb) at 91 J. Grade B (Ti) exhibits the highest impact toughness, exceeding 101 J. This behaviour can be attributed to dilution effects between the WM and the differently microalloyed BM, resulting in varying chemistries of the WM and consequently influencing its toughness. The comparatively high impact energies observed in the WM samples can be attributed primarily to the predominance of acicular ferrite (AF), a microstructural constituent well recognised for its superior toughness relative to bainitic transformation products [ 26 ]. Furthermore, the extent of BM dilution and its intermixing with the welding wire played a decisive role. In this context, the degree of dilution is defined by the relationship between the initial weld geometry and the final fusion boundary, and it is quantified through metallographic cross sections [ 9 ], indicating the fraction of BM that was melted during welding. Across all four welds investigated, the average dilution was 41%, implying that a substantial portion of the alloying elements from the respective BMs was incorporated into the solidified WM [ 4 ]. Consequently, the resulting variations in WM chemistry exerted a pronounced influence on the impact toughness. For instance, it is well established that Ti and its associated precipitates act as highly effective nucleation sites for the formation of AF, thereby enhancing toughness [ 27 ,  28 ].

When examining the maximum local strains in the WM, an opposite trend compared to the HAZ becomes apparent. In the welded reference grade, the local strain in the WM reached approximately 45% (Fig.  11 b), while strain predominantly accumulates in the HAZ, where higher values are observed (Fig.  11 a). In grade A (Nb), strain accumulates mainly in WM and exceeds 87%. Grade B (Ti) shows a similar tendency; however, the local strain in WM was 43%, with most of the strain concentrated in HAZ (Fig.  11 a). In contrast, the assessment of local strain in WM of grade C (Ti + Nb) shows a large deviation. This microalloying concept caused varying deformation behaviour among the three tensile specimens, and no consistent fracture location could be identified. The strain in WM is comparable to that in HAZ and reaches approximately 81%.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: The following study investigated the influence of different Ti and Nb microalloying on weld and HAZ properties of four S690QL-like steel grades. By combining a multi-step approach (of metallographic characterisation, hardness testing, thermophysical simulation, DIC-based characterisation of cross-weld tensile samples and Charpy impact toughness), the relationship between the microalloying influence on the HAZ softening, local strain distribution, and fracture behaviour was evaluated. The following conclusions can be drawn: Ti and/or Nb microalloying addition (grades A to C) effectively suppressed the AG growth caused by the pinning effect of the forming precipitates on the AG boundaries. At a peak temperature of 1200 °C, the average grain diameter was reduced by approximately 47% for the Nb-microalloyed grade and by about 70% for the Ti-containing grades compared to the reference steel. In that connection, the Ti precipitates exhibited the highest thermal stability (grades B and C), whereas the reference alloy without Ti and Nb showed no significant restriction of AG growth. The hardness reductions in the IC- and SCHAZ regions strongly depended on the microalloying strategy. The combined Ti + Nb microalloying approach (grade c) resulted in the smallest softened zone and exhibited a high tempering resistance during the multipass welding, whereas the reference grade and Ti-only variant (grade B) developed more pronounced softening zones. Statistical models further indicated that high Ti and/or Nb contents can even promote intensified softening. However, these findings apply specifically to the hardness distribution in the filler layer of the three-layer weld. Independently of the microalloying concept, all welded joints exhibit comparable UTS values (between 829 and 848 MPa) and total elongation (from 6.5 to 7.8%). However, the final fracture consistently occurred in locally softened HAZ regions or in the vicinity along the fusion line. DIC measurements revealed pronounced constraint effects. The Ti + Nb alloying concept (grade C) exhibited the highest local strain in the HAZ (> 80%), whereas Nb-alloying (grade A) resulted in the accumulation of the strains in the WM (> 87%). Therefore, the microalloying concept is of high interest as it has direct impact on the plastic strain localisation and the onset of fracture. The Ti + Nb alloying concept (grade C) exhibited the highest Charpy impact toughness values in HAZ (> 148 J at −40 °C) and the highest local HAZ strain (> 80%), whereas the reference material (without Ti and Nb) showed significantly decreased performance. In WM, the Ti-microalloyed variant (grade B) achieved the highest toughness (> 100 J), promoted by both the Ti-induced AF formation and the specific dilution between the individual BM and G69 filler material.
